items.title: Context
items.body:
What is outside SpecPad, and how each boundary is reached.

- **A git repository** — the only durable store. SpecPad writes files into `docs/specpad/` and reads
  history through the `git` binary. There is no database anywhere in the product.
- **The browser's File System Access API** — how the hosted editor reaches a local checkout. Absent in
  Firefox and Safari, so every write path has an upload/download fallback.
- **A SpecPad server** (optional) — holds the clone on behalf of someone with no checkout, and speaks
  the same document operations over HTTP.
- **Claude Code** — runs the skill, which edits the same files programmatically.
- **An eQMS** — consumes exported evidence. Out of scope for the software itself.

The invariant across all four: the *files* are the interface. Any actor that can read and write the
JSON and markdown under `docs/specpad/` is a first-class client.

items.title: Composition
items.body:
How the units below group into the architecture's blocks (see the SAD building-block view).

| Block | Units |
|---|---|
| Shared contract | schema, docTypes, validate, governance, ids, factories, diff, merge, verification, launcher |
| Editor shell | LocalApp, fileApi, transports (local/demo/remote), launchParams, theme, handleStore |
| Editor views | register tables, TestingView, ArchitectureView, JobsView, ReleasesView, Auditor, Traceability, Overview, chrome |
| Editor derivations | changeTracking, archDiff, auditReport, designControls, outline |
| Server | config, registry, routing, auth, paths, git, repository, workingCopy, commitGate, api, entry point, presence, events, branchWatcher |
| Skill | SKILL.md procedures, templates, verification adapter, mirror sync |

Grouping is by *what changes together*, not by directory: `fileApi` sits with the shell rather than
the transports because it owns file conventions, which change with the document set rather than with
the storage medium.

items.title: Dependency
items.body:
Dependency direction, and the one rule that matters: **everything depends on the shared contract; the
contract depends on nothing.**

- Editor → `src/shared`. Server → `src/shared`. Skill mirrors the contract *in prose* and is held to
  it by a parity test rather than an import, because it is a prompt, not a program.
- No edge runs the other way. A contract module that needed to know about a view or an endpoint would
  mean the rule the editor and the server are supposed to share had been split in two.
- The server declares no copy of validation, governance, merge or diff — enforced by
  `server/__tests__/contract-parity.test.ts`, the same guard the skill has.

Acceptance: both parity tests pass, and `src/shared` imports nothing from `src/`, `server/` or
`site/`.

items.title: Information model
items.body:
What SpecPad stores, and what it refuses to store.

Every document shares an envelope — `schemaVersion`, `type`, `name`, `title` — and register
documents carry an ordered `items[]`. An item has a **stable id** and an optional renameable **code**.
References always target ids: `verifies` → SRS, `satisfies` → PRD, `design` → SDD.

Three refusals, each load-bearing:

- **No history fields.** No author, no modified date, no changelist. Git owns history; anything stored
  would be a second, wrong copy.
- **Nothing derived.** Test counts, result roll-ups, release→job mapping and coverage are computed on
  read. A stored roll-up is a cache that can disagree with its source.
- **No reverse links.** The reverse of every trace is derived when the matrix is rendered, so there is
  exactly one place to maintain each edge.

The regenerable caches under `.specpad/` look like an exception and are not: they hold verbatim past
copies of these same files, never derived data, and can be rebuilt from git at any time.

items.title: External interfaces
items.body:
The four boundaries the software crosses, and what each guarantees.

- **`FileApi`** (`src/transports/types.ts`) — four methods: `listDocuments`, `readJson`,
  `readText`, `writeText`. Absent is `null`, never an exception; an unreadable path is absent too,
  so one bad diagram reference cannot abort opening a project. Every transport passes one conformance
  suite.
- **HTTP API** (`/api/v1/…`, optionally under `/p/<project>`) — mirrors those operations, plus
  session, status, commit, discard, presence, events. Refusals carry data the UI renders (a 409 commit
  result), which is why they are not thrown.
- **The git CLI** — every git call goes through an injectable runner, so the pipeline is testable
  without a repository and there is exactly one place where the process boundary is crossed.
- **Server-sent events** — advisory presence and an upstream-moved signal. Failure of this interface is
  defined as normal: the editor says less.

items.title: Conventions used throughout
items.body:
Rules applied in many units, written once here rather than repeated in each.

- **Ids are generated once and immutable** — a typed prefix plus six hex digits (`r_`, `t_`, `p_`,
  `d_`, `h_`, `j_`), unique within a file, from `ids.ts`. Nothing else may mint an id.
- **Codes are labels.** Renaming a code is always safe, because nothing resolves by code. Where a legacy
  commit trailer used a code instead of an id, matching it back requires an end-anchored search — an
  unanchored `JOB-3` also matches `JOB-35`.
- **Governance is opt-in per pillar.** A rule that depends on an optional register only runs when that
  register is present, so a project that does not use PRD or SDD pays nothing.
- **Advisory features never block.** Presence, the branch watcher, and the project switcher all degrade
  to silence rather than to an error.
- **Absent, refused and broken are three different answers**, and conflating them is the defect this
  convention exists to prevent.

items.title: Degradation and failure behaviour
items.body:
How the software behaves when something it depends on is missing — the design decisions that let one
codebase serve a static host, a local checkout, and a server.

- **No File System Access API** → upload/download fallback, and in server mode the API is used instead,
  so a Firefox user on a server saves normally rather than silently downloading a file.
- **No `EventSource`** → presence subscription becomes a no-op.
- **No server** → the session probe must distinguish a real server from a static host answering an
  unknown path with `index.html`; it requires JSON *and* a session shape.
- **An unresolvable diagram reference** → the project still opens, with that diagram missing.
- **An unreachable project on a multi-project server** → the other projects still serve.

Acceptance: each degraded path has a test asserting the *degraded* behaviour, not merely the absence of
a crash.

items.title: schema — types and JSON Schemas
items.body:
Secret: the wire format. Every document type's TypeScript type and JSON Schema live here together, so
the two cannot drift apart.

Interface: `projectSchema`, `srsSchema`, `vtpSchema`, `prdSchema`, `sddSchema`, plus the
matching types and `SCHEMA_VERSION`.

Structure only — no policy. Whether a reference *resolves* is governance's job, not the schema's;
mixing them would put half the rules where the editor can enforce them and half where it cannot.
Descriptions on every property are load-bearing: the published schema reference is generated from them.

Acceptance: every schema validates its factory's output; every property carries a description
(`schema-descriptions.test.ts`).

items.title: docTypes — the document-type registry
items.body:
Secret: **which content document types exist**, and how each behaves — register / prose / asset,
optional, in-baseline, generated.

This is the extensibility mechanism. Validation, the schema reference, snapshots, per-job diffs, the
redline, and the generator all iterate the registry, so adding a pillar is a registration plus a schema
rather than an edit in each of those places. Adding the SDD exercised exactly that: no snapshot, diff or
generator code changed.

Interface: `DOC_TYPES`, `REGISTER_TYPES`, `docTypeFor`, `isRegisterType`,
`registerTypesInIndex`. An unknown type resolves to `undefined` rather than throwing — callers treat
unknown types as "not mine".

Acceptance: a newly-registered type flows into snapshots, per-job diffs, redline and the generator with
no other change (`docTypes.test.ts`).

items.title: validate — structural validation
items.body:
Secret: how a document is checked against its schema, and which schema applies to which `type`.

Interface: `validate(doc) → string[]`. An empty array means structurally valid. It returns *every*
problem rather than the first, because an author fixing one error at a time is the slowest way to fix
five.

Deliberately says nothing about policy: a document can be structurally perfect and still violate
traceability. Keeping the two separate is what lets the schema stay a pure description of shape.

Acceptance: valid fixtures return `[]`; each malformed fixture names its own field.

items.title: governance — policy
items.body:
Secret: **the rules that make a document set trustworthy**, as opposed to merely well-formed —
traceability, referential integrity, expected results, active-job discipline, and the opt-in PRD and SDD
rules.

Interface: `GOVERNANCE_RULES` (the canonical list) and `checkGovernance(bundle) → violations`. Pure
over data, which is what lets the editor, the skill and the server all run it and never disagree; the
skill is held to the same list by a parity test.

Rules that need `HEAD` — "spec changes require an active job" — deliberately live in the skill's
pre-commit gate instead, because a browser has no git.

Opt-in rules run only when their register is present. Where a rule has a rigor dimension (the SDD), it
is checked at maximum rigor unconditionally; omission is an export decision.

Acceptance: each rule has a test that trips it and one that does not; the skill documents every rule id.

items.title: ids — identity
items.body:
Secret: the id format, and that it is random rather than sequential.

Interface: `generateId(prefix, existing)` and `ID_PREFIX`. Collides-and-retries against the ids
already in the file; gives up after a bounded number of attempts rather than looping forever.

Random, not sequential: two people adding an item offline must not mint the same id, and a sequential
counter is state that would have to be stored and merged.

Acceptance: generated ids match the typed-prefix format and never collide with the supplied set.

items.title: factories — new documents and items
items.body:
Secret: what a *new* empty document and a *new* item look like, including which fields are seeded.

Interface: `createProjectDoc`, `createSrsDoc`, `createVtpDoc`, `createSddDoc`, and the per-item
factories. The project factory builds `documents[]` from the registry, so a newly registered pillar is
part of the default document set without touching this unit.

Acceptance: every factory's output validates; new items carry a fresh unique id.

items.title: diff — item-level comparison
items.body:
Secret: what "changed" means for an id-keyed register — added, removed, modified, keyed on id, with
order never counting as a change.

Interface: `diffItems(before, after)`, `diffDocs`, `valuesEqual`. Exported `valuesEqual` is why
"changed" means one thing everywhere: the redline, the merge and the pending-change summary all use it.

Reordering is not a change. Treating it as one would make every reorder look like a rewrite of the whole
document.

Acceptance: reordering yields no differences; a field change yields exactly one modified item.

items.title: merge — three-way structural merge
items.body:
Secret: **that SpecPad documents are merged by item id, never as text.** A line-based merge of a
formatted JSON array produces plausible-looking garbage — duplicated ids, orphaned references, silently
dropped items — and the failure is invisible in review.

Interface: `mergeDocs(base, ours, theirs) → { doc, conflicts }`. Pure. Changes to different fields of
one item combine; a conflict is raised only where both sides set the same field differently, or one side
deletes what the other modified. Order is never a conflict.

Invalid input: a document that is not an id-keyed register is refused rather than merged.

Acceptance: different-field edits combine with no conflict; same-field edits conflict; a delete-modify
pair conflicts; no output ever contains conflict markers.

items.title: verification — run matching
items.body:
Secret: how a VTP item's `automation` links resolve against a captured run — and that SpecPad is
framework-agnostic, treating `runner` and `selector` as opaque.

Interface: the matcher and result derivation — automated tests derive passed/failed/skipped/not-run from
the run; manual tests fall back to a stored result; roll-ups computed, never stored.

A link with no matching result is **not run**, which is distinct from failed. Collapsing those two would
make a missing test look like a passing one or a broken one, and neither is true.

Acceptance: each status derives correctly; an unmatched link reports not-run.

items.title: launcher — where the editor lives
items.body:
Secret: the mapping from contract version to editor build path — `"1.0"` → `/v01/` — and that it is
*derived*, never configured.

Interface: `editorVersionPath`, `editorUrl`, `DEFAULT_EDITOR_BASE`. A blank or absent base falls
back to the hosted editor, so an existing project is untouched. The server imports this rather than
deriving its own copy.

Invalid input: a `schemaVersion` with no numeric major throws at once, rather than producing a path
that would 404 later.

Acceptance: the version path is derived from the contract; a configured base changes the host but never
the version segment.

items.title: LocalApp — the editor shell
items.body:
Secret: how a session gets from "a page loaded" to "a project is open" — and which of the three
transports it is talking to.

Owns the open project, the active view, the loaded document set and every piece of derived state the
views read. On load it probes for a server, then the demo, then falls back to local files.

Deliberately the only place that decides *where* documents come from; a view never knows.

Invalid input: an unopenable project sets an error and leaves the editor closed rather than half-loaded.

Acceptance: each of the three entry paths opens a project; switching documents re-seeds the tables;
navigation between views preserves the loaded set.

items.title: fileApi — document conventions
items.body:
Secret: **SpecPad's file conventions** — which filename holds the SRS, where a snapshot lives, what
"absent" means for an optional sidecar — kept separate from *how* bytes are read.

Interface: the load/save functions every view uses, plus the server-mode operations. Delegates all I/O to
the active `FileApi`.

This split is why adding a transport changed no view, and why adding a document type changes no
transport.

Acceptance: the same conventions hold across all three transports (one conformance suite).

items.title: local transport — File System Access
items.body:
Secret: the browser's directory-handle model, including permission re-prompting and the upload/download
fallback where the API is unavailable.

Invalid input: a revoked or stale handle is reported as "not open" rather than throwing at the first
read, so the editor can offer to re-pick the folder.

Acceptance: passes the transport conformance suite; a persisted handle reopens without a picker when its
grant survived.

items.title: demo transport — read-only hosted content
items.body:
Secret: that the demo is a static file listing fetched over HTTP, and that it is read-only.

Every write is refused with a message naming the demo, rather than failing at the storage layer, so the
UI never has to special-case demo mode.

Acceptance: reads resolve against the manifest; every write is refused.

items.title: remote transport — a SpecPad server
items.body:
Secret: the HTTP protocol, and the optimistic-concurrency bookkeeping — version tags seen on read are
replayed on write so a stale edit is refused by the server rather than silently overwriting someone.

Interface: the `FileApi` methods plus session, status, commit, discard, presence, events, and project
discovery. The API base carries the project (`/api/v1/p/<id>`), so the same transport serves a
single-project and a multi-project deployment.

Invalid input, and the distinction that caused a real defect: **404 is absent (null); 409 is a refusal
carrying data** the dialog renders. Conflating them returned the error body as though it were the
document.

Acceptance: passes the conformance suite; a stale write is refused; a refused commit yields renderable
data; the probe is not fooled by a static host.

items.title: launchParams — reading the launch URL
items.body:
Secret: that the local folder path travels in the URL *fragment*, which browsers never send to a server,
while `demo` and `project` are read from the query string.

Invalid input: an unrecognised view name is ignored rather than opening a broken tab.

Acceptance: fragment and query forms both parse; an invalid `open` value is dropped.

items.title: theme — appearance
items.body:
Secret: the token layer. Themes are CSS custom properties under `[data-theme]`, so a new theme is a
block of variables rather than a sweep through component styles.

Applied pre-paint by an inline script so there is no flash of the wrong theme, and persisted to
localStorage. An unknown stored theme falls back to the default rather than rendering unstyled.

Acceptance: each theme applies; an unknown persisted value degrades to the default.

items.title: handleStore — recent projects
items.body:
Secret: that directory handles persist in IndexedDB, and that a persisted handle may have lost its
permission grant.

Interface: remember, list, and re-verify. Unsupported browsers get an empty list, never an error.

Acceptance: a remembered project reappears; a handle whose grant lapsed is offered for re-picking rather
than silently failing.

items.title: changeTracking — redline and attribution
items.body:
Secret: how a redline is computed from two snapshots, and how attribution is assembled from a sequence
of them — entirely on read, from committed verbatim copies.

Interface: `buildRedline`, `computeAttribution`, and the cached-release helpers. Pure over documents,
so there is no git in the browser and no stored diff anywhere.

Missing snapshot: yields no redline rather than an empty one, so "unchanged" and "unknown" stay
distinguishable.

Acceptance: a redline matches the underlying item diff; attribution orders by snapshot sequence.

items.title: archDiff — section-level markdown diff
items.body:
Secret: that architecture changes are reported by *heading section* rather than by line, because "§6
Runtime View changed" is what a reviewer can act on and "line 214 changed" is not.

Interface: `mdSectionDiff(before, after)`. Diagrams stay coarse — changed or not — deliberately: no
regulator tracks in-diagram deltas, and semantic diagram diffing is a research problem.

Acceptance: a reworded paragraph reports its section; an unchanged document reports nothing.

items.title: auditReport — coverage and roll-ups
items.body:
Secret: how coverage, the trace matrix and test roll-ups are computed — including that automated results
come from the *run*, not from a stored field.

Interface: `buildAuditReport(docs, run)`. Run-aware by construction: passing the run in was the fix for
roll-ups that broke when stored results were cleared in favour of captured ones.

Acceptance: roll-ups match the run; a requirement with no test is reported unverified.

items.title: designControls — the regulatory map
items.body:
Secret: the mapping from design-control elements to where their evidence lives, with IEC 62304 and
21 CFR 820.30 citations — deliberately in core rather than in the medical add-on, because a reviewer's
first question ("where are your design inputs?") must be answerable in any project.

Interface: `buildDesignControls(docs)` → elements with a live status of present / partial / gap.

Status is derived, never stored, so it cannot claim evidence that is no longer there.

Acceptance: a project missing a pillar reports that element as a gap.

items.title: outline — heading hierarchy
items.body:
Secret: how a flat `items[]` with `level` renders as a numbered hierarchy, and how a heading's dotted
code is composed from its ancestors.

Keeping items flat is what makes reordering, diffing and merging simple; the tree exists only at render
time.

Acceptance: nested headings compose dotted codes; a flat document is unaffected.

items.title: Register tables — SRS, VTP, PRD
items.body:
Secret: the editing model for an id-keyed register — inline edit, row actions, expandable reference
cells, redline decoration, and presence markers.

Three tables rather than one generic one, deliberately: each register has a different set of columns
that matter, and the shared abstraction that would cover all three was worse than the duplication.

Invalid input: an edit that would break a reference is prevented at the cell rather than saved and
reported later.

Acceptance: each table edits its register, renders its redline, and surfaces its own trace column.

items.title: TestingView — the evidence chain
items.body:
Secret: the presentation of the chain **VTP item → automated test → captured run**, including run
provenance and the manual-result fallback.

Automated rows show a derived badge and are not hand-editable; manual rows keep a control. Making the
derived value editable would let someone type a passing result over a failing run.

Acceptance: a run-backed row shows the derived status; a manual row keeps its stored result; an
unmatched link shows not-run.

items.title: ArchitectureView — authoring and display
items.body:
Secret: that the SAD is markdown with diagrams *placed inline by the document*, and that editing and
display are separate sub-views (CodeMirror; react-markdown with SVGs resolved from the project folder).

Invalid input: an unresolvable diagram reference renders as missing and never aborts opening the project.

Acceptance: referenced diagrams render inline; a missing one degrades locally.

items.title: JobsView — change tracking
items.body:
Secret: how a job's impact is assembled for display — per-document-type diffs from the frozen caches,
architecture changes, commits, and the verification roll-up — plus the active job's *in-progress* diff
against its before-snapshot.

Iterates the registered document types, so a new pillar's changes appear here with no edit. That is how
SDD changes show up in a job.

Acceptance: a closed job renders its diffs and commits; the active job renders uncommitted changes; a new
register type appears without code change.

items.title: ReleasesView — release notes
items.body:
Secret: that a release's job list is *derived* from each job's version rather than stored, and grouped
for reading as release notes.

Acceptance: jobs group under their release; unreleased work is shown as such.

items.title: Auditor and Traceability views
items.body:
Secret: the split between *orientation* (the design-control map: which formal element lives where) and
*evidence* (the trace matrix, coverage and gaps). They were one view and were separated because a
reviewer arriving cold needs the map first.

Both render a scope disclaimer: this is evidence supporting design controls, not a quality system.

Acceptance: the map links to each tab; the matrix flags unverified requirements and unresolved links.

items.title: OverviewView — the landing view
items.body:
Secret: which four things answer "what is the state of this project" — coverage headline, in-progress
jobs, latest release, quick jumps — and that all four are derived on read.

Acceptance: renders from documents alone; degrades cleanly when an optional pillar is absent.

items.title: Editor chrome — menubar, tabs, status, server bar, dialogs
items.body:
Secret: the navigation model — tabs grouped and ordered by design-control phase, with phase bands above
them — and the server-session affordances.

The tab strip is a CSS grid rather than a list so a band can span several tabs. The ServerBar answers
who am I, what may I do, how much is unpublished, and which project. The CommitDialog shows the pending
change set at **item** level plus the governance result *before* anything is committed.

A row menu renders in a portal so it cannot be clipped by the table it sits in.

Acceptance: tabs and bands render for the available document set; a reader is offered no Commit; the
dialog renders refusals and conflicts rather than discarding them.

items.title: DetailedDesignView — the design tab
items.body:
Secret: how a *sectioned prose* register is edited — an outline beside one section at a time, with
Display and Edit sub-views, the same shape the Architecture tab uses. A row-per-section table was
rejected: a markdown body with an embedded flowchart does not belong in a table cell.

The load-bearing part is neither pane. Every section shows **which requirements reference it**,
derived on read from `SrsItem.design`, which is the re-review rule made visible: editing a section
warns that those requirements are now in question, and deleting one names exactly what it would
leave dangling. Without that, the rule exists only in a guide nobody has open at the time.

Invalid input: a section with no body renders as empty rather than blank-but-broken; an unresolvable
diagram reference names the missing file, exactly as the architecture view does.

Acceptance: sections list and open; the referencing requirements appear on the section and in the
edit warning; a delete names the requirements it would break and abandons on cancel; identity
survives every edit; read-only mode offers no editing affordance at all.

items.title: server/config — the deployment declaration
items.body:
Secret: the shape of a deployment — projects, identity, roles, commit policy, working-copy lifecycle —
and that validation is exhaustive and startup-blocking.

Interface: `validateConfig` (collects every problem) and `loadConfig` (throws with all of them).

Invalid input is the main behaviour: a half-configured server holding push access to a real repository is
worse than one that refuses to start. A single-repository config is still accepted and read as a
one-project deployment.

Acceptance: a valid config yields resolved projects; each malformed field is named; every problem is
reported at once.

items.title: server/registry — the hosted projects
items.body:
Secret: that per-project state is *per project* — one clone, presence registry, event bus and branch
watcher each — and that one unreachable repository must not stop the others being served.

Interface: `get`, `list`, `sole`, `ensureClones` (returns failures rather than throwing), `tick`,
`reapIdle`, `closeAll`.

Acceptance: each project gets its own runtime; a failing clone is reported and the others still serve.

items.title: server/routing — which project a request is for
items.body:
Secret: the URL shape `/p/<id>/…`, and the rule that an unnamed project resolves **only** when the
deployment has exactly one.

Pure string functions, so the routing rule is testable without a server, a clone, or a request.

Invalid input: an unknown project is a 404; no project named on a multi-project server is a 400 carrying
the list, never an arbitrary choice.

Acceptance: prefixed and unprefixed paths resolve per the rule; the ambiguous case refuses.

items.title: server/auth — identity and authorization
items.body:
Secret: **that SpecPad implements no authentication.** An upstream the company already runs asserts the
identity; providers normalise it to one `Principal`, and nothing downstream knows which provider ran.

Also secret, and separate: **identity is not the git credential.** The human is the commit *author*; a
machine credential does the push.

Authentication is deployment-wide, authorization is per project, so they are two steps: `authenticate`
then `sessionFor(principal, roles)`. No role in one project says nothing about another.

Invalid input: header-asserted identity from an untrusted peer is ignored outright; the dev provider
refuses any non-loopback bind.

Acceptance: each provider yields a principal or null; role precedence picks the strongest match; an
untrusted peer cannot assert an identity.

items.title: server/paths — path confinement
items.body:
Secret: the client-path grammar, and that **every function here is a security control**.

Client paths are relative to the project root; there is deliberately no way to express an absolute path
or a parent traversal. Absolute paths and `..` are refused outright rather than reinterpreted, because
silently serving a reinterpreted path hides the caller's bug.

Second line of defence: sparse-checkout means the tree physically cannot contain application source.

Acceptance: traversal, absolute, null-byte and drive-letter forms are each refused; the staged diff is
re-checked before a commit.

items.title: server/git — git plumbing
items.body:
Secret: the git command surface, behind an injectable runner so the pipeline is testable without a
repository.

Interface: `run` (throws) and `tryRun` (returns a result) — the distinction matters because "the file
does not exist at this ref" is an ordinary answer, not an error.

Never force-pushes. Note the subtlety in `conflictedFile`: during a *rebase* git's index stages are
inverted relative to how a user thinks about them; this unit returns them the way the user means.

Acceptance: commands compose against a fake runner; a rebase conflict reports the right side as "theirs".

items.title: server/repository — clone and worktrees
items.body:
Secret: the on-disk layout — one bare clone per project, one sparse worktree per user under
`workDir/projects/<id>/` — and the worktree lifecycle.

Provisioning is serialized so two concurrent requests cannot race one worktree, and lazy so a user who
never opens a project costs nothing.

Reaping has two refusals that are the point of the unit: a copy holding **uncommitted changes** is never
removed (that work exists in no git object), and a copy the process has **not seen used** is never
removed (so a restart cannot delete everyone's drafts).

Acceptance: sparse checkout excludes source; two users get independent copies; an idle clean copy is
reaped; a dirty one never is; a reaped copy is re-provisioned invisibly.

items.title: server/workingCopy — reads, writes, publication
items.body:
Secret: the commit pipeline — stage, gate, commit as the human, rebase, retry, push — and the structural
conflict resolution that replaces a textual merge.

Interface: read/write/list, `status`, `pendingDiff` (item-level, so the dialog can say "REQ-14
modified" rather than name a file), `publish`, `discard`.

Invalid input: a refused commit returns an outcome describing the refusal; it never throws, because the
refusal is data the dialog renders. Nothing is ever force-pushed, and no document ever ends up holding
conflict markers.

Acceptance: an autosaved edit is pending and absent from the repository until Commit; two people editing
different requirements both land; same-field edits conflict without loss.

items.title: server/commitGate — validate and govern before publishing
items.body:
Secret: what must be true before a change may enter the repository — structural validity, governance,
an active job — and the policy that decides whether a violation blocks or warns.

Pure function over the changed documents plus policy, which is what makes it testable without git.

**Runs server-side because the client is not trusted.** For someone who will never run the test suite,
this gate *is* the dogfood rule.

Acceptance: an invalid document is blocked; a governance breach blocks under `block` and warns under
`warn`; a change with no active job is refused when the policy requires one.

items.title: server/api — the HTTP surface
items.body:
Secret: the endpoint set and **where authorization is enforced** — here, not in the browser. The
editor's read-only rendering is a courtesy; a reader's write request is refused server-side regardless
of what the client chose to display.

Interface: session, documents, status, doc/text read and write, commit, discard, presence.

Invalid input: a bad path becomes 400; a missing document 404; a stale write 409 carrying the current
version; an unknown endpoint 404 naming the method and path.

Acceptance: each endpoint enforces its capability; a reader is refused a write; a stale write is refused.

items.title: server entry point — process and static serving
items.body:
Secret: that one process serves the version-pinned editor build **and** the API from a single origin —
which is what removes CORS, third-party cookies, cross-domain redirects, and any dependency on
specpad.com being reachable inside a corporate network.

Also owns shutdown, and the non-obvious part: an open SSE stream never ends on its own, so the streams
must be ended before `close()` or the process hangs until it is killed.

Invalid input: an invalid config exits non-zero with every problem listed, having listened on nothing.

Acceptance: the process starts from a config file and answers over HTTP end to end; SIGTERM shuts down
without hanging; static paths never escape the build directory.

items.title: server/presence, events, branchWatcher — advisory signals
items.body:
Secret: **that all three are deliberately weak**, and the design decisions that keep them from becoming
load-bearing.

Claims expire on their own after 45 seconds; nothing blocks on them; losing the registry to a restart
costs a moment of silence. A lock that vanishes when someone shuts a laptop lid must never be
load-bearing.

The branch watcher's two non-events are the interesting part: a first observation is not a change, and an
unreachable remote is not a change. Either mistake would tell every open editor to reload for nothing.

Events are scoped per project, so a claim in one project cannot wake another's subscribers. Dead
subscribers are dropped rather than thrown.

Acceptance: claims expire unreleased; a repeated heartbeat does not re-broadcast; a dying sink is
dropped; a malformed frame is ignored; cross-project events are not delivered.

items.title: The skill — procedures as a prompt
items.body:
Secret: that the skill is **prose, not a program** — an agent procedure with no CLI — and that this is a
deliberate distribution choice, not an unfinished one.

It mirrors the contract in words: the same governance rule ids, the same file conventions, the same id
discipline. Nothing enforces that at compile time, so a parity test holds it to the shared module.

Contains the working loop, `init`, the baseline generator, the requirement audit, change-tracking cache
maintenance, the release-cut procedure, and verification-run capture.

Acceptance: every governance rule id appears in SKILL.md; every shipped guide is routed to and no guide
body is inlined.

items.title: Templates and the pre-push hook
items.body:
Secret: what a newly scaffolded project contains, and the enforcement backstop.

The launcher template is generated per project: it hardcodes no editor host, substituting both the base
URL and the optional server project id in *both* the redirect and the no-JavaScript fallback — a
launcher that redirects correctly but links wrongly is worse than one consistently wrong, because the
fallback is what a blocked-script user sees.

The pre-push hook blocks a commit with no `Job:` trailer and warns on code without spec. It skips
merges, tag pushes and pre-adoption history, and has an explicit waiver and bypass, because a gate with
no escape hatch gets disabled entirely.

Acceptance: the launcher substitutes both occurrences; the hook blocks, warns, skips and waives as
specified.

items.title: Verification adapter and tooling
items.body:
Secret: the boundary between SpecPad and a test framework. The adapter converts one runner's machine
report into the normalized run record; the core never parses a test framework, so another runner is a
sibling adapter rather than a change to the contract.

`sync-skill` mirrors the distributable skill into the repo's own `.claude/skills/` so this repo runs
the skill it ships. The mirror is committed and gated on push, because a mirror that can drift is worse
than none.

Acceptance: a vitest run produces a valid run record whose links resolve; the mirror matches the source.

items.title: Marketing site and generated reference
items.body:
Secret: that the published schema reference is **generated from the live contract at build time**, not
maintained by hand — which is why it cannot describe a version of the schema that does not exist.

A second Vite build, deployed to the apex while the editor is deployed under its version path.

Acceptance: the reference is generated from the registry and its schemas; site links resolve.
